rv.q: Lyle Kessler’s harrowing play, about two imperfectly socialized brothers living like feral animals in a rundown neighborhood of North Philadelphia, acquires unexpected emotional nuance under Daniel Sullivan’s incisive helming.
The production feels undernourished, lacking the muscular intensity and emotional depth that might have made this a more compelling evening.

If these words are not too strange to use about a very dark power play about feral brothers and a violent kidnapping, "Orphans" is a giddy delight -- an acting treat, a fast-talking adrenaline jolt and lots of fun.
In the end what we remember is Sturridge’s astonishing turn.
It's become a dismayingly rare pleasure to see a serious play on Broadway, and while this revival, like "Orphans" itself, is far from perfect, it's still very much worth seeing.
Not that it’s a bad play. It’s just weirdly trifling.
This is a play more fun to act in than watch.
Yet this version somehow plays like a sentimental sitcom, perhaps a low-rent “Modern Family.”

Director Daniel Sullivan makes the fatal mistake of trusting a play that is just an excuse for actors to fling themselves around a squalid set and out-emote each other. The airy, far-too-clean space only shows up Orphans' contrivances. Foster and Sturridge are both commendable-physically robust, emo...
They make this simple story feel both real and somehow larger than life.
It's a shame that it took 30 years to bring this briskly entertaining, deeply affecting play to Broadway; but at least Orphans has arrived in good hands.

Sturridge is phenomenal as Phillip, the type of fellow we’d think of today as falling somewhere on the autistic spectrum, though such classifications likely weren’t part of Kessler’s vernacular back in the day.
Although the unusual scenario that it explores is engaging at first, it eventually runs out of steam and inspiration.
“Orphans” remains as synthetic as ever, only now Tom Sturridge, Ben Foster, and Alec Baldwin do the bravura thesping.
On Broadway in 2013, Orphans is not so much menacing as meagre.
In its Broadway premiere, we get to see some of those thespian fireworks, but the full impact of Kessler’s shattering tale of little boys lost is lost amid the craving for audience affection.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this revival of Kessler's play, praising the actors' fierce performances and Sullivan's direction, but many find the script itself derivative and dated, calling it synthetic Pinter-meets-Shepard that hasn't aged well.

vs.sum: The Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, although some side seats may have partial views. The sound quality is generally strong, enhancing the theatrical experience. However, the seating is tight, which can affect comfort, particularly for taller patrons. The theater's ambiance is charming with its historic character, and while facilities are adequate, expect some lines at the bar and restrooms.

acc.note: 7 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra. Infrared devices available.
